$g ( f\left(x\right) )$ is continuous

at $x = - a \text{ and }$ at $x = 0$

$f\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}x + 2, & x < 0 \\ {x}^{2}, & x \ge 0\end{cases}\right$ and $g\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}{x}^{3}, & x < 1 \\ 3x - 2, & x \ge 1\end{cases}\right$

Then, the number of points in $R$ where $\left(fog\right)\left(x\right)$ is NOT differentiable is equal to :
questions.explanation:
$f\left(g\left(x\right)\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}g\left(x\right) + 2, & g\left(x\right) < 0 \\ {\left(g\left(x\right)\right)}^{2}, & g\left(x\right) \ge 0\end{cases}\right$

$= \left\{\begin{cases}{x}^{3} + 2, & x < 0 \\ {x}^{6}, & x \in [ 0, 1 ) \\ {\left(3x - 2\right)}^{2}, & x \in [ 1, \infty )\end{cases}\right$

${\left(fog\left(x\right)\right)}^{'} = \left\{\begin{cases}3{x}^{2}, & x < 0 \\ 6{x}^{5}, & x \in [ 0, 1 ) \\ 2\left(3x - 2\right) \times 3, & x \in [ 1, \infty )\end{cases}\right$

At $x = 0$

$L . H . L . \ne R . H . L .$ (Discontinuous)

At $x = 1$

$L . H . L . = R . H . L .$ (continuous)

$L . H . D . = 6 = R . H . D .$

$⇒ fog\left(x\right)$ is differentiable for all $x \in R - \left\{0\right\}$

Let $f: R\toR$ be defined as $f\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}2sin\left(- \dfrac{\pix}{2}\right), & ifx 1\end{cases}\right$

If $f\left(x\right)$ is continuous on $R$, then $a + b$ equals :
questions.solution:
$f\left(x\right)$ is continuous on $R$

$⇒ f\left({1}^{-}\right) = f\left(1\right) = f\left({1}^{+}\right)$

$\left|a + 1 + b\right| = \lim_{x \to {1}^{+}}sin\left(\pi x\right)$

$\left|a + 1 + b\right| = 0 ⇒ a + b = - 1$

$⇒$ Also

$f\left(- {1}^{-}\right) = f\left(- 1\right) = f\left(- {1}^{+}\right)$

$\lim_{x \to - 1}2sin\left(\dfrac{- \pix}{2}\right) = \left|a - 1 + b\right|$

$\left|a - 1 + b\right| = 2$

Either $a - 1 + b = 2$ or $a - 1 + b = - 2$

from $\left(1\right)$ and $\left(2\right)$⇒ a + b = 3 = - 1$ (reject)

from $\left(1\right)$ and $\left(3\right)$⇒ a + b = - 1$

questions.q: Let $f$ be any function defined on $R$ and let it satisfy the condition: $\left|f\left(x\right) - f\left(y\right)\right| \le \left|{\left(x - y\right)}^{2}\right|, ∀ \left(x, y\right) \in R$. If $f\left(0\right) = 1,$ then :
questions.solution:
$\left|\dfrac{f\left(x\right) - f\left(y\right)}{\left(x - y\right)}\right| \le \left|\left(x - y\right)\right|$

Let $x - y = h$

$⇒ x = y + h$

$\lim_{x \to 0}\left|\dfrac{f\left(y + h\right) - f\left(y\right)}{h}\right| \le 0$

$⇒ \left|{f}^{'}\left(y\right)\right| \le 0 ⇒ {f}^{'}\left(y\right) = 0$

$⇒ f\left(y\right) = k$ (constant)

And $f\left(0\right) = 1$ given

So, $f\left(y\right) = 1 ⇒ f\left(x\right) = 1$

questions.q: The number of points, at which the function $f\left(x\right) = \left|2x + 1\right| - 3\left|x + 2\right| + \left|{x}^{2} + x - 2\right|, x \in R$ is not differentiable, is
questions.solution:
$f\left(x\right) = \left|2x + 1\right| - 3\left|x + 2\right| + \left|{x}^{2} + x - 2\right|$

$= \left|2x + 1\right| - 3\left|x + 2\right| + \left|x + 2\right|\left|x - 1\right|$

$= \left|2x + 1\right| + \left|x + 2\right|\left(\left|x - 1\right| - 3\right)$

Critical points are $x = \dfrac{- 1}{2}, - 2, - 1$

but $x = - 2$ is making a zero twice in product so, points of non differentiability are $x = \dfrac{- 1}{2}$ and $x = - 1$

$∴$ Number of points of non-differentiability $= 2$

questions.q: If the function $f\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}{k}_{1} ( x - \pi{)}^{2} - 1, & x \le \pi \\ {k}_{2}cosx, & x > \pi\end{cases}\right$ is twice differentiable, then the ordered pair $\left({k}_{1}, {k}_{2}\right)$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
$f ( x )$ is differentiable then will also continuous then $f ( \pi ) = {k}_{1}{\left(\pi - \pi\right)}^{2} - 1 = - 1$

$f\left({\pi}^{+}\right) = \lim_{h \to 0}{k}_{2}cos\left(\pi + h\right) = - {k}_{2}$

$f\left({\pi}^{+}\right) = f\left(\pi\right) ⇒ {k}_{2} = 1 \ldots \left(1\right)$,$f$ is continuous.

Now, $f ' ( x ) = \left\{\begin{cases}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left\{{k}_{1} ( x - \pi{)}^{2}\right\}, & x \le \pi \\ \dfrac{d}{dx}\left\{{k}_{2}cosx\right\}, & x > \pi\end{cases}\right$

$f ' ( x ) = \left\{\begin{cases}2{k}_{1} ( x - \pi ) , & x \le \pi \\ - {k}_{2}sinx, & x > \pi\end{cases}\right$

then, $f ' \left({\pi}^{-}\right) = 2{k}_{1}\left(\pi - \pi\right) = 0$

$f ' \left({\pi}^{+}\right) = - {k}_{2}sin\left(\pi\right) = 0$

$⇒ f ' \left({\pi}^{-}\right) = f ' \left({\pi}^{+}\right) = 0$

Similarly, we get

$f ' ' ( x ) = \left\{\begin{cases}2{k}_{1}, & x \le \pi \\ - {k}_{2}cosx, & x > \pi\end{cases}\right$

As the function is twice differentiable, the second-order derivatives, $LHD = RHD$

$⇒ f ' ' \left({\pi}^{-}\right) = f ' ' \left({\pi}^{+}\right) ⇒ 2{k}_{1} = - {k}_{2}cos \pi$

$⇒ 2{k}_{1} = {k}_{2}$

$⇒ {k}_{1} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ (from $\left(1\right)$)

questions.q: Let $f ( x ) = x \cdot \left[\dfrac{x}{2}\right],$ for $- 10 < x < 10,$ where $\left[t\right]$ denotes the greatest integer function. Then the number of points of discontinuity of $f\left(x\right) is equal to$
questions.solution:
We know that the greatest integer function is discontinuous at integral points.

$- 5 < \dfrac{x}{2} < 5$

$⇒ \left[\dfrac{x}{2}\right] = - 5, - 4, - 3, - 2, - 1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$, are the integer values.

At $x = 0$, $f\left({0}^{+}\right) = f\left(0\right) = f\left({0}^{-}\right) = 0$, which means that function is continuous at $x = 0$.

$∵ x \ne - 10 ⇒ \dfrac{x}{2} \ne - 5$

Hence, the function is discontinuous at points $- 4, - 3, - 2, - 1, 1, 2, 3, 4$

The number of values is $8$ .

questions.q: Let $f: ( 0, \infty ) \to ( 0, \infty )$ be a differentiable function such that $f ( 1 ) = e$ and $\lim_{t \to x}\dfrac{{t}^{2}{f}^{2} ( x ) - {x}^{2}{f}^{2} ( t )}{t - x} = 0 .$ If$f ( x ) = 1$, then $x$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
$\lim_{t \to x}\dfrac{{t}^{2}{f}^{2} ( x ) - {x}^{2}{f}^{2} ( t )}{t - x} = 0$
Using L'Hospital

$\lim_{t \to x}\dfrac{2t{f}^{2} ( x ) - {x}^{2}2f ( t ) {f}^{'} ( t )}{1} = 0$
$⇒ 2x{f}^{2} ( x ) - {x}^{2}2f ( x ) {f}^{'} ( x ) = 0$
$⇒ 2xf ( x ) [ f ( x ) - x{f}^{'} ( x ) ] = 0$
But $f ( x ) \ne 0$

So, $x{f}^{'} ( x ) = f ( x )$
$⇒ x\dfrac{dy}{dx} = y$
$⇒ \dfrac{1}{y}dy = \dfrac{1}{x}dx$
Integration gives

$lny = lnx + lnc$
$⇒ y = cx ⇒ f ( x ) = cx$
Now

$f ( 1 ) = c = e$ (given)

So, $f ( x ) = ex$
Now if $f ( x ) = 1$, then $ex = 1 ⇒ x = \dfrac{1}{e}$

questions.q: If a function $f\left(x\right)$ defined by $f\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}a{e}^{x} + b{e}^{- x}, & - 1 \le x < 1 \\ c{x}^{2}, & 1 \le x \le 3 \\ a{x}^{2} + 2cx, & 3 < x \le 4\end{cases}\right$be continuous for some $a, b, c \in R$ and ${f}^{'}\left(0\right) + {f}^{'}\left(2\right) = e$, then the value of $a$ is
questions.solution:
Continuous at $x = 1, 3$

$f\left({1}^{-}\right) = f\left(1\right) ⇒ ae + b{e}^{- 1} = c . . . ( 1 )$

$f\left(3\right) = f\left({3}^{+}\right) ⇒ 9c = 9a + 6c ⇒ c = 3a . . . \left(2\right)$

From $\left(1\right)$ and $\left(2\right)$

$b = ae ( 3 - e ) . . . \left(3\right)$

${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}a{e}^{x} - b{e}^{- x}, & - 1 < x < 1 \\ 2cx, & 1 < x < 3 \\ 2ax + 2c, & 3 < x < 4\end{cases}\right$

${f}^{'}\left(0\right) = a - b, {f}^{'}\left(2\right) = 4c$

Given ${f}^{'} ( 0 ) + {f}^{'} ( 2 ) = e$

$a - b + 4c = e . . . \left(4\right)$

questions.q: Let $f: R \to R$ be differentiable at $c \in R$ and $f\left(c\right) = 0$. If $g\left(x\right) = \left|f\left(x\right)\right|$, then at $x = c, g$ is:
questions.solution:
Given $g\left(x\right) = \left|f\left(x\right)\right|$ and $f\left(c\right) = 0$

${g}^{'}\left({c}^{+}\right) = \lim_{x \to {c}^{+}}\dfrac{\left|f\left(x\right)\right| - f\left(c\right)}{x - c} = \lim_{x \to {c}^{+}}\left|\dfrac{f\left(x\right) - f ( c )}{x - c}\right|, asx > c$

$⇒ {g}^{'}\left({c}^{+}\right) = \left|{f}^{'}\left(c\right)\right|$

$g\left({c}^{-}\right) = \lim_{x \to {c}^{-}}\dfrac{\left|f\left(x\right)\right| - f\left(c\right)}{x - c} = - \lim_{x \to {c}^{-}}\left|\dfrac{f\left(x\right) - f ( c )}{x - c}\right|, asx < c$

$⇒ {g}^{'}\left({c}^{-}\right) = - \left|{f}^{'}\left(c\right)\right|$

For $g\left(x\right)$ to be differentiable at $x = c$, ${f}^{'}\left(c\right)$ must be $0$. Else, it is non-differentiable.

questions.solution:
$∵ f\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{array}{ll}sin ⁡ \left(p + 1\right)x + sinx x\end{array} q \dfrac{\sqrt{{x}^{2} + x} - \sqrt{x}}{{x}^{3 / 2}} \begin{array}{ll}: x 0\end{array}\right$

$∵ f$ is continuous at $x = 0$

$L . H . L =$

$\lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{sin\left(p + 1\right)\left(- h\right) + sin ( - h )}{- h} = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{sin\left(p + 1\right)h + sinh}{h}$

$= \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{sin\left(p + 1\right)h}{h\left(p + 1\right)}\left(p + 1\right) + \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{sinh}{h} = p + 1 + 1$

$= p + 2$

$R . H . L = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{\sqrt{{h}^{2} + h}-\sqrt{h}}{h\dfrac{3}{2}} \times \dfrac{\sqrt{{h}^{2} + h} + \sqrt{h}}{\sqrt{{h}^{2} + h} + \sqrt{h}} = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{{h}^{2} + h - h}{h\dfrac{3}{2}h\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{h + 1} + 1\right)}$

$\lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 + h} + 1} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$⇒ L . H . L . = R . H . L . = f\left(0\right) ⇒ p + 2 = \dfrac{1}{2} = q$
$= \begin{array}{ll}p = - \dfrac{3}{2} \text{ and } q = \dfrac{1}{2}\end{array}$

questions.solution:
For continuity at $x = 5$

$\lim_{x \to {5}^{+}}f\left(x\right) = \lim_{x \to {5}^{-}}f\left(x\right) = f\left(5\right)$

$⇒ \lim_{x \to {5}^{+}}\left(b\left|x - \pi\right| + 3\right) = \lim_{x \to {5}^{-}}a\left(\left|\pi - x\right| + 1\right) = a\left(5 - \pi\right) + 1$

We know that $\left|x\right| = \left\{\begin{cases}x, & x \ge 0 \\ - x, & x < 0\end{cases}\right$

$⇒ b\left(5 - \pi\right) + 3 = a\left(5 - \pi\right) + 1 = a\left(5 - \pi\right) + 1$

$⇒ b\left(5 - \pi\right) + 3 = a\left(5 - \pi\right) + 1$

$⇒ 3 - 1 = a\left(5 - \pi\right) - b\left(5 - \pi\right)$

$⇒ \left(a - b\right)\left(5 - \pi\right) = 2$

$⇒ a - b = \dfrac{2}{5 - \pi} .$

questions.q: Let $f\left(x\right) = 15 – \left|x – 10\right|; x \in R .$ Then the set of all values of $x$, at which the function $g\left(x\right) = f ( f\left(x\right) )$ is not differentiable, is:
questions.solution:
$f\left(x\right) = 15 - \left|x - 10\right|$

$⇒ g\left(x\right) = f\left(f\left(x\right)\right)$

$⇒ g\left(x\right) = 15 - \left|f\left(x\right) - 10\right|$

$= 15 - \left|15 - \left|x - 10\right| - 10\right|$

$= 15 - \left|5 - \left|x - 10\right|\right|$

$= 15 - \left|\left|x - 10\right| - 5\right|$

We know that, $\left|x\right| = \left\{\begin{cases}x, & x \ge 0 \\ - x, & x < 0\end{cases}\right$

Case $1:$

When $x < 10$

$g\left(x\right) = 15 - \left|10 - x - 5\right|$

$⇒ g ( x ) = 15 - \left|5 - x\right|$

Now if $x < 5$, then $g\left(x\right) = 15 - 5 + x = x + 10$

And if $x \ge 5$, then $g ( x ) = 15 + 5 - x = 20 - x$

Case $2:$x \ge 10$

$g\left(x\right) = 15 - \left|x - 10 - 5\right|$

$⇒ g ( x ) = 15 - \left|x - 15\right|$

Now if $10 \le x < 15$

$⇒ g\left(x\right) = 15 - 15 + x$

So, $g\left(x\right) = x$

Now for $x \ge 15$, then $g\left(x\right) = 15 - x + 15 = 30 - x$


$g\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}x + 10, & x < 5 \\ 20 - x, & 5 \le x < 10 \\ x, & 10 < x \le 15 \\ 30 - x, & x \ge 15\end{cases}\right$

Now, it is clear from the graph of $g\left(x\right)$ has sharp corners at$x = 5, 10, 15$ and hence this function is not differentiable at $x = 5, 10, 15 .$

questions.solution:
Given $f\left(1\right) = 2$ and $f\left(x + y\right) = f\left(x\right) \cdot f\left(y\right)$

Put $x = y = 1$

$⇒ f\left(2\right) = f\left(1\right) \cdot f\left(1\right) = {2}^{2}$

Now, put $x = 1, y = 2$

$⇒ f\left(3\right) = f\left(1\right) \cdot f\left(2\right) = {2}^{3}$

Now, put $x = 1, y = 3$

$⇒ f\left(4\right) = f\left(1\right) \cdot f\left(3\right) = {2}^{4}$

Similarly, $f\left(10\right) = {2}^{10}$

Now $\mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{10}f\left(a + k\right) = 16\left({2}^{10} - 1\right)$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{10}f\left(a\right)f\left(k\right) = 16\left({2}^{10} - 1\right)$

$⇒ f\left(a\right)\mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{10}f\left(k\right) = 16\left({2}^{10} - 1\right)$

$⇒ f\left(a\right)\left(f\left(1\right) + f\left(2\right) \ldots + f\left(10\right)\right) = 16\left({2}^{10} - 1\right)$

$⇒ f\left(a\right)\left({2}^{1} + {2}^{2} + {2}^{3} + \ldots + {2}^{10}\right) = 16\left({2}^{10} - 1\right)$

Using the sum of $n$ terms of a geometric progression, i.e. $a + ar + a{r}^{2} + a{r}^{3} + . . . + a{r}^{n - 1} = \dfrac{a\left({r}^{n} - 1\right)}{r - 1},$ we get

$f\left(a\right)\dfrac{2\left({2}^{10} - 1\right)}{2 - 1} = 16\left({2}^{10} - 1\right)$

$⇒ f\left(a\right) = 8 = {2}^{3}$

Also, we know that $f\left(3\right) = 8$

$⇒ f\left(a\right) = f\left(3\right)$

$⇒ a = 3 .$

$= \left\{\begin{array}{ll}- x - 1; - 1 \le x < 0 \\ x + 0; 0 \le x < 1 \\ 2x; 1 \le x < 2 \\ x + 2; 2 \le x < 3 \\ 6; x = 3\end{array}\right$

Let $\mathrm{K}$ be the set of all real values of $x$ where the function $f(x)=\sin |x|-|x|+2(x-\pi) \cos |x|$ is not differentiable.

Then the set $K$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
$f(x)=\sin |x|-|x|+2(x-\pi) \cos |x|$

There are two cases,

Case $(1), x>0$f(x)=\sin x-x+2(x-\pi) \cos x$f^{\prime}(x)=\cos x-1+2(1-0) \cos x-2 \sin (x-\pi)$f^{\prime}(x)=3 \cos x-2(x-\pi) \sin x-1$

Then, function $f(x)$ is differentiable for all $x>0$

Case $(2) x  < 0$f(x)=-\sin x+x+2(x-\pi) \cos x$f^{\prime}(x)=-\cos x+1-2(x-\pi) \sin x+2 \cos x$f^{\prime}(x)=\cos x+1-2(x-\pi) \sin x$

Then, function $f(x)$ is differentiable for all $x < 0$

Now check for $x=0$f^{\prime}\left(0^{*}\right) \mathrm{R} \cdot \mathrm{HD}=3-1=2$f^{\prime}(0) \mathrm{L} . \mathrm{H.D.}=1+1=2$\mathrm{L} . \mathrm{HD}=\mathrm{R} . \mathrm{H.D}$

Then, function $f(x)$ is differentiable for $x=0 .$ So it is

differentiable everywhere

Hence, $k=\phi$

Let $f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cl}-1, & -2 \leq x  < 0 \\ x^{2}-1, & 0 \leq x \leq 2\end{array}\right.$ and

$g(x)=|\eta(x)|+f(x \mid) .$ Then, in the interval $(-2,2), g$ is:
questions.solution:
$f(x)=\left\{ \begin{array}{cc}-1, & -2 \leq x  < 0 \\ x^{2}-1, & 0 \leq x \leq 2\end{array} \right. \text{ Then, } f(x \mid)=\left\{ \begin{array}{cc}

-1, & -2 \leq|x| < 0 \\

|x|^{2}-1, & 0 \leq|x| \leq 2

\end{array} \right. \Rightarrow f(|x|)=x^{2}-1,-2 \leq x \leq 2 \Rightarrow g(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned} 1+x^{2}-1, &-2 \leq x < 0 \\\left(x^{2}-1\right)+\left|x^{2}-1\right|, & 0 \leq x \leq 2 \end{aligned}\right. =\left\{\begin{array}{cc}x^{2}, & -2 \leq x < 0 \\ 0, & 0 \leq x < 1 \\ 2\left(x^{2}-1\right), & 1 \leq x \leq 2\end{array}\right. g^{\prime}\left(0^{-}\right)=0, g^{\prime}\left(0^{*}\right)=0, g^{\prime}\left(1^{-}\right)=0, g^{\prime}\left(1^{+}\right)=4 \Rightarrow g(x)$ is non-differentiable at $x=1 \Rightarrow g(x)$ is not differentiable at one point.

questions.q: Let $f$ be a differentiable function from $R to R$ such that $\left|f\left(x\right) - f\left(y\right)\right| \le 2{\left|x - y\right|}^{3 / 2},$ for all $x, y \in R\text{.}$ If $f\left(0\right) = 1$ then $\mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}{f}^{2}\left(x\right)dx$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given functional equality is

$\left|f\left(x\right) - f\left(y\right)\right| \le 2{\left|x - y\right|}^{3 / 2}$

Put $x = y + h,$ we get

$\left|f\left(y + h\right)\right| - f\left(y\right){\left|\le 2 . | h\right|}^{3 / 2}$

$⇒ \left|\dfrac{f\left(y + h\right) - f ( y )}{h}\right| \le 2{\left|h\right|}^{1 / 2}$

$⇒ \lim_{h \to 0} ⁡ \left|\dfrac{f\left(y + h\right) - f\left(y\right)}{h}\right| \le \lim_{h \to 0} ⁡ 2{\left|h\right|}^{1 / 2}$

$⇒ \left|{f}^{′}\left(y\right)\right| \le 0$

$⇒ \left|{f}^{′}\left(y\right)\right| = 0$

$⇒ f′\left(y\right) = 0$

$⇒ f\left(y\right) = c$

$⇒ f\left(y\right) = 1$ (since $f\left(0\right) = 1$ )

Now ${∫}_{0}^{1}{f}^{2}\left(x\right)dx = {∫}_{0}^{1}1dx = 1$.

questions.q:
Let $f: R \to R$ be a function defined as

$f\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{array}{ll}5, ifx \le 1 \\ a + bx, if1 < x < 3 \\ b + 5x, if3 \le x < 5 \\ 30, ifx \ge 5\end{array}\right$

Then $f$ is:
options: not continuous for any values of  $a$  and  $b$
questions.solution:
$f\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{array}{ll}5: x \le 1 \\ a + bx: 1 < x < 3 \\ b + 5x: 3 \le x < 5 \\ 30: x \ge 5\end{array}\right$

For $f ( x )$ to be continuous at $x = 5$

$\lim_{x \to {5}^{-}}f\left(x\right) = \lim_{x \to {5}^{+}}f\left(x\right) = f\left(5\right)$

$⇒ \lim_{x \to {5}^{-}}\left(b + 5x\right) = 30$

$⇒ b + 25 = 30 ⇒ b = 5$

For $f ( x )$ to be continuous at $x = 1$

$\lim_{x \to {1}^{+}}f\left(x\right) = \lim_{x \to {1}^{-}}f\left(x\right) = f\left(1\right)$

$⇒ \lim_{x \to {1}^{+}}\left(a + 5x\right) = 5$

$⇒ a = 0$

Now at $x = 3,$

$LHL = \lim_{x \to {3}^{-}}\left(0 + 5x\right) = 15$

$RHL = \lim_{x \to {3}^{+}}\left(5 + 5x\right) = 20$

Hence function $f ( x )$ is discontinuous at $x = 3$ for all $a, b \in R$ .

questions.solution:
Given $f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{1}{x} - \dfrac{k - 1}{{e}^{2x} - 1}, x \ne 0$

and $f\left(x\right)$ is continuous at $x = 0$.

$⇒ f\left(0\right) = \lim_{x \to 0}\left(\dfrac{1}{x} - \dfrac{k - 1}{{e}^{2x} - 1}\right)$

$= \lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{\left(1 + \left(2x\right) + \dfrac{1}{2 !}{\left(2x\right)}^{2} + \ldots \left(- 1 - x\left(k - 1\right)\right)\right)}{2{x}^{2}\left(\dfrac{{e}^{2x} - 1}{2x}\right)}$

$= \lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{\left(1 + \left(2x\right) + \dfrac{1}{2 !}{\left(2x\right)}^{2} + \ldots \left(- 1 - x\left(k - 1\right)\right)\right)}{2{x}^{2}}$

Clearly, $k = 3$ and $f\left(0\right) = 1$. $($∵$Equating coefficient of $x = 0$)$

questions.q: Let $S=\left\{(\lambda, \mu) \in R \times R: f(t)=\left(|\lambda| e^t-\mu\right) \cdot \sin (2|t|)\right.$, $t \in R$, is a differentiable function $\}$. Then $S$ is a subest of?
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}&\quad S=\left\{(\lambda, \mu) \in \mathrm{R} \times \mathrm{R}: \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{t})=\left(|\lambda| \mathrm{e}^{\mid t}-\mu\right) \sin (2 \mathrm{t} \mid),\right.\\
&t \in \mathbb{R} \\
&f(t)=\left(|\lambda| \mathrm{e}^{|t|}-\mu\right) \sin (2|t|) \\
&\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\left(|\lambda|e^t-\mu\right) \sin 2 t \quad t>0 \\
\left(|\lambda|e^{-t}-\mu\right)(-\sin 2 t) t < 0
\end{array}\right. \\
&f^{\prime}(t) \\ \left\{\begin{array}{l}
\left(|\lambda| \mathrm{e}^t\right) \sin 2 t+\left(|\lambda| \mathrm{e}^t-\mu\right)(2 \cos 2 t) t>0 \\
|\lambda| \mathrm{e}^{-t} \sin 2 t+\left(|\lambda|e^{-t}-\mu\right)(-2 \cos 2 t) < t < 0
\end{array}\right. \\
 \text{ As, }$ f(t) $\text{$ is differentiable }\\
&\therefore $\text{ LHD }=\mathrm{RHD} \text{ at }  t=0 \\
&|\lambda| $\cdot \sin2(0)+$\left(|\lambda| \mathrm{e}^0-$\mu\right)^{2}$\cos  (0) \\
&=|\lambda| \mathrm{e}^{-0}$ \cdot \sin2(0)-2 $\cos$(0)$\left(|\lambda| \mathrm{e}^{-0}-$\mu\right)$\\
&\Rightarrow 0+(|\lambda|-\mu)^{2}=0-2(|\lambda|-\mu) \\
&\quad 4(|\lambda|-\mu)=0 \\
&\quad|\lambda|=\mu
\end{aligned}

So, $ S \equiv(\lambda, \mu)=\{\lambda \in $\mathbb{R}$ \& \mu \in[0, \infty)\}$
Therefore set  \mathrm{S}$ is subset of $R \times[0, \infty) $

$f\left(x\right) = \left|x - \pi\right| . \left({e}^{\left|x\right|} - 1\right) . sin\left|x\right|$

$L{f}^{′}\left(\pi\right) = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{f\left(\pi\right) - f\left(\pi - h\right)}{h} = - \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{\left|- h\right|sin ⁡ \left(\pi - h\right)\left({e}^{\pi - h} - 1\right)}{h} = 0$

Differentiable at $x = \pi$

$R{f}^{′}\left(0\right) = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{f\left(h\right) - f\left(0\right)}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0}\left|h - \pi\right| \times \dfrac{sin\left|h\right|\left({e}^{\left|h\right|} - 1\right)}{h} = 0$

$L{f}^{′}\left(0\right) = \lim_{h \to 0} ⁡ \dfrac{f\left(0\right) - f\left(- h\right)}{h} = - \lim_{h \to 0}\left|- h - \pi\right| \times \dfrac{sin\left|- h\right|\left({e}^{\left|- h\right|} - 1\right)}{h} = 0$

Hence, $f\left(x\right)$ is differentiable everywhere.

$⇒ S = ϕ$

questions.solution:
We know that if $y \le {k}^{2}, ⇒ - k \le y \le k, k \in R .$

Given $\left|f\left(x\right)\right| \le {x}^{2}, ∀ x \in R$

$⇒ - {x}^{2} \le f\left(x\right) \le {x}^{2} ∀ x \in R$

Now, $\lim_{x \to 0}{\left(- x\right)}^{2} = \lim_{x \to 0}\left({x}^{2}\right) = 0,$

Hence, by using sandwich theorem, $\lim_{x \to 0}f\left(x\right) = 0$

Further $\left|f\left(0\right)\right| \le 0 ⇒ f\left(0\right) = 0$

Since, $\lim_{x \to 0}f\left(x\right) = f\left(0\right) = 0$

Hence, $f\left(x\right)$ is continuous at $x = 0$

Now, if $x \ne 0,$ then $- \left(x\right) \le \dfrac{f\left(x\right)}{\left(x\right)} \le \left(x\right)$

Thus, by using sandwich theorem, we have $\lim_{x \to 0} - \left(x\right) \le \lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{f\left(x\right)}{\left(x\right)} \le \lim_{x \to 0}\left(x\right)$

$⇒ 0 \le \lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{f\left(x\right)}{\left(x\right)} \le 0$

$⇒ \lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{f\left(x\right)}{\left(x\right)} = 0 . . . \left(i\right)$

We know that a function $f\left(x\right)$ is differentiable at a point $x = a,$ if $\lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{f\left(a - h\right) - \left(a\right)}{- h} = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{f\left(a + h\right) - \left(a\right)}{h}$

Now, the left-hand derivative at $x = 0$ is

$\lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{f\left(0 - h\right) - f\left(0\right)}{- h} = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{f\left(- h\right)}{- h} = 0,$ ( by using equation $\left(i\right)$)

And, the right-hand derivative at $x = 0$ is

$\lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{f\left(0 + h\right) - f\left(0\right)}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{f\left(h\right)}{h} = 0,$ ( by using equation $\left(i\right)$)

Hence, $f\left(x\right)$ is differentiable at $x = 0 .$

f(u)=$\frac{1}{u^2+u-2}=\frac{1}{(u+2)(u-1)},$which is discontinous at $u=-2,1$

when $u=1$, then $\frac{1}{x-1}=1 \Rightarrow x=2$

Statement 1: $\lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{-}} f(x)$ exists.
Statement 2: $f$ is continuous at $x=2$.
options:
Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true, Statement 2 is a correct explanation for Statement 1.

Statement 1 is false, Statement 2 is true.

$\begin{aligned}$& $\text{ Consider } \frac{x}{[x]} \leq$f(x) \leq $\sqrt{6-x}$\\
& \Rightarrow $\lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{-}} \frac{x}{[x]}=\frac{2}{1}=$2
\end{aligned}

$\begin{aligned}$& \Rightarrow $\lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{-}} \sqrt{6-x}=$2 \\
& \therefore $\lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{-}}$f(x)=2
\end{aligned}

[By Sandwich theorem]
Now $\lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{+}} \frac{x}{[x]}=1, \lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{+}} \sqrt{6-x}=2$
Hence by Sandwich theorem $\lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{+}} f(x)$ does not exists.

questions.q: Let $f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}(x-1) \sin\left(\frac{1}{x-1}\right), & \text{ if } x \neq 1 \\ 0, & \text{ if } x=1\end{array}\right.$. Then which one of the following is true?
options:
$f$ is neither differentiable at $x=0$ nor at $x=1$ 

$f$ is differentiable at $x=0$ and at $x=1$

$\mathrm{f}$ is differentiable at $\mathrm{x}=0$ but not at $\mathrm{x}=1$

$\mathrm{f}$ is differentiable at $\mathrm{x}=1$ but not at $\mathrm{x}=0$
questions.solution:
$
f^{\prime}(1)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}
$

$
\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow f^{\prime}(1)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{(1+h-1) \sin \left(\frac{1}{1+h-1}\right)-0}{h}=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{h}{h} \sin \left(\frac{1}{h}\right) \\
& \Rightarrow f^{\prime}(1)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \sin \left(\frac{1}{h}\right)
\end{aligned}
$
$\therefore \mathrm{f}$ is not differentiable at $x=1$.
Similarly, $f^{\prime}(0)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h}$\Rightarrow f^{\prime}(0)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{(h-1) \sin \left(\frac{1}{h-1}\right)-\sin (1)}{h}$\Rightarrow \mathrm{f}$ is also not differentiable at $\mathrm{x}=0$.
